grammarPoints.title: Wanting to do something: たい
grammarPoints.meaning: Express your own wishes, ask about the listener’s wishes, or carefully report another person’s wishes.
grammarPoints.formation: Verb masu-stem + たいです. Inflect たい like an i-adjective: たくない, たかった, たくなかった. For someone else: 〜たいと言っていました or observed stem + たがっています.
notes: A direct object can take を or が with たい; other verb particles stay the same. With たがっている, retain を, not が.
Use a direct statement of たい mainly for yourself and a question for the listener. A third person’s private wish needs a report or observed behavior.
たいと思っています can express a wish you have held for some time.

grammarPoints.title: Listing sample activities with たり
grammarPoints.meaning: Mention some activities without claiming that the list is complete or giving a fixed order.
grammarPoints.formation: Verb past short form + り、verb past short form + り + する. Conjugate the final する for the sentence’s tense and register.
notes: The た in each たり does not make the whole sentence past. します versus しました sets the time.
Unlike a simple sequence of te-forms, the list presents examples without ordering them. Keep the final する.

grammarPoints.title: Life experience with たことがある
grammarPoints.meaning: Say that an event has occurred in your experience, or that it never has.
grammarPoints.formation: Affirmative past short verb + ことがあります / ことがありません. Question: ことがありますか.
notes: Negate あります for “never”; the verb before こと stays affirmative past.
This reports experience, not a just-completed task. まだ〜ていません instead presents an expected task as pending.
A short reply is あります/ありません. Do not reply with ことがあります by itself.

grammarPoints.title: Giving noun examples with や
grammarPoints.meaning: Give two or more examples from a larger set of things.
grammarPoints.formation: Noun A や noun B + the particle required by the rest of the sentence.
notes: や connects nouns, not full clauses or conjugated verbs. Use たり for sample activities.
と can suggest a complete list; や leaves other members unmentioned.

grammarPoints.title: Extra: は in negative statements
grammarPoints.meaning: Mark what you are denying or contrasting, often by using は where an affirmative sentence used を or が.
grammarPoints.formation: Object/topic は + negative predicate. With に or で, add は after the particle: には, では.
notes: This is a common preference, not a rule that all negative sentences must use は. を and が can still be grammatical.
Do not replace a destination’s に or a means marker で with は when their role is still needed.

grammarPoints.title: Extra: a limited quantity with だけ
grammarPoints.meaning: Say that the quantity is just the stated amount, with no more added.
grammarPoints.formation: Number + counter + だけ. Put the quantity in its usual position in the sentence.
notes: Use the correct counter for the object. This practice uses the general small-object つ series.
だけ itself does not require a negative verb. Do not introduce しか, which belongs later.

grammarPoints.title: Extra: an occasion marked by に
grammarPoints.meaning: Identify an occasion such as a meal at which an action occurs.
notes: Here に marks the occasion, not a destination or the item being eaten.
Keep the food object separately marked with を.
